1	# Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya
2	
3	> Status: draft v3, for owner review · Updated: 2026-11-09
4	> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Each layer ends with what it costs engineers and
5	> what it gives Compliance.
6	
7	## How to read this
8	
9	Eight layers. Each has a **Principle** (tool-independent), **On Papaya's stack** (Pulumi,
10	Serverless Framework, GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s, Claude Code) and **Audit evidence** (records an
11	auditor can test without asking anyone). Copy-paste detail belongs in `examples/`.
12	
13	| Marker | Meaning |
14	|---|---|
15	| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented. R*x.y* is a ✅/📖 row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes or links the official page (a few rows cite vendor blogs, bulletins or example files instead, e.g. R2.4.1b, R6.3.5, R5.5.4). |
16	| ⚠️ R*x.y* | Inference, open question or "What this means for Papaya" conclusion in the research (sections 1.8, 2.9, 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, 5.6, 5.7, 6.5), or the ⚠️ part of a mixed row. Reasoned, not documented. |
17	| ⚠️ | Not verified at all, e.g. an illustrative command. |
18	| [design] | My proposal, built from documented parts, untested. Treat as ⚠️. |
19	
20	Nothing here was checked locally (✅): this is a design without access to Papaya's systems.
21	**GĐ-n** = assumption in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4 (owner-confirmed: GĐ-1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11,
22	14; the others are marked "unconfirmed" where used); **S-n** = success criteria
23	(§5); **P/A-n** = problems (§1); **D1–D3** = owner decisions in research 6.6; **Options §n** =
24	`work/03-options.md`; **G-n** = gaps; **OD-n** = owner decisions on this draft (both at the end).
25	Earlier owner answers are cited with their source: "research 6.9.4 Q4", "framing Q8", "Options §9 Q2".
26	
27	---
28	
29	## 1. The decision in one page
30	
31	Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
32	of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.
33	
34	**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):
35	
36	1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
37	   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
38	2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets an approved grant
39	   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h, ⚠️ R2.9 #3) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
40	3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.
41	
42	| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
43	|---|---|
44	| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
45	| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |
46	| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
47	| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |
48	
49	**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**
50	
51	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
52	  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
53	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
54	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
55	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
56	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
57	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
58	  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
59	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
60	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
61	  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
62	  laptops it is enforced by policy and training, not by a technical control: an agent could approve
63	  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.
64	- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
65	  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
66	  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). The cost: GitHub accepts an
67	  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve another
68	  domain's PR. Domain review on normal days becomes a process rule with a monthly check, not a
69	  technical control. Because on-call approvers only
70	  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
71	  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
72	- **One approver for high-risk changes.** L3 changes (IAM, stateful deletes, workflow files) get one
73	  approver, like L2, but the path is owned by the L3 owner team (or by the stack's owners for L3
74	  content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at
75	  the prod preview (OD2, OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off
76	  for speed.
77	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
78	  business associate, as the brief implies.
79	
80	**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):
81	
82	1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
83	   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
84	2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
85	3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
86	4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.
87	
88	### Roles
89	
90	| Role | Rule |
91	|---|---|
92	| Author (engineer + their agent) | Never approves own change; GitHub blocks PR authors from approving (📖 R3.3.1). |
93	| Approver | Always an engineer, never an agent (owner rule, OD5). Named in CODEOWNERS; ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3); for an app-opened PR, ≠ the person who triggered it (⚠️ R3.3.4, layer 5). |
94	| Incident responder | Engineer who diagnoses and writes the fix or the JIT request. Never the on-call approver of the same shift (OD7). |
95	| On-call approver | Engineer on the on-call schedule, primary + backup, 24/7; wait ≤ 15 min (S7). While on call they only approve: they write no fix and file no JIT request, so the approver is always distinct from the author (OD7). The primary approves; the backup replaces an unavailable primary (OD2). No platform-team membership is required; all engineers follow one agreed approval procedure (OD2). |
96	| Data owner [design] | Named per tenant; co-approves real-data reads, or reviews a night-time read the next working day (layer 6). |
97	| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1); owns policies and metrics; not the only approver. |
98	
99	---
100	
101	## Layer 1 — Identity and access
102	
103	**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
104	written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
105	to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.
106	
107	**On Papaya's stack**
108	
109	- **The engineer's access is the agent's access.** The agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and
110	  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse
111	  detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate
112	  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
113	  holds.
114	- **Process rules** that follow from this:
115	  - the JIT terminal runs no agent, though the grant is reachable from the same laptop (owner
116	    accepted as a process control, D2);
117	  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles (D2; `--restricted` per D3,
118	    research 6.9.4 Q2);
119	  - the real-data terminal runs no agent when the store holds PHI [design], same weakness as D2;
120	  - an agent never approves PRs: an owner rule (OD5), enforced on laptops by policy and training.
121	    GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
122	    excerpt read names "approving Claude's own pull request" (📖 R6.3.3); whether approving
123	    someone else's PR is blocked is unverified (⚠️), and the list
124	    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no
125	    documented meaning, R3.5.6).
126	- **IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1) [design names]:
127	  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim
128	    stores; 1 h session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). Until a service's logs are redacted at source
129	    (layer 6), it gets that service's metrics only. Lambda configuration can hold secrets resolved by
130	    Serverless in plain text (⚠️ R4.4.7), so configuration reads are allowed per service only after
131	    its secrets move to runtime resolution (⚠️ R4.6 #7). Cost: until then the agent reads
132	    timeout/memory from the IaC code;
133	  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad, non-prod accounts only;
134	  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: assigned only by the JIT flow (layer 7), via a partner product, the
135	    TEAM sample (📖 R2.4.1, R2.4.1b) or a small home-built flow (⚠️ R2.4.2) on the documented APIs
136	    `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2);
137	  - no standing prod-write permission set.
138	- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
139	  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
140	    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
141	    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
142	  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
143	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
144	    JIT roles. This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
145	    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (key 📖 R4.4.5; need ⚠️ R4.6 #3);
146	  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:UserId` (📖 R2.4.4); protect the org trail (📖 R2.6.2).
147	  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
148	    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path, held by the L3 owner team only, not co-owned by the on-call group; part of AR 2).
149	- **Sessions/MFA:** portal session length set on purpose; an IdP session can extend it silently
150	  (📖 R2.1.5, R2.1.6). MFA lives in the external IdP if one is used (📖 R2.1.7).
151	- **CI → AWS:** GitHub OIDC, no stored keys (📖 R3.4.1). The prod role trusts only the `production`
152	  environment of the monorepo, in its `sub` format (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4; immutable format assumed,
153	  ⚠️ R3.7 A2), ideally customised with the deploy workflow's `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
154	- **CI → GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization, which Google
155	  requires (📖 R3.4.5b).
156	- **k0s, GCP and Firebase for humans:** same principles; mechanisms not researched (G1–G3). Today
157	  k0s is reached with kubeconfigs, no SSO (GĐ-4, unconfirmed). Interim: no admin kubeconfig and no GCP
158	  owner role on laptops; prod deploys only from CI. Firebase is not on the GCP BAA list (📖 R5.5.3), so
159	  Firebase Hosting must hold no PHI (⚠️ R5.7 #7).
160	
161	**Audit evidence.** Identity Center assignment export (S1); CloudTrail `CreateAccountAssignment` /
162	`DeleteAccountAssignment` per grant (📖 R2.4.2), linked to its approval by request ID [design]; SCPs
163	and trust policies as Pulumi code; IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` on policy PRs
164	(📖 R2.8.1); quarterly access review of permission sets and GitHub admins.
165	
166	**Cost / value.** Engineers lose standing prod write and keep a free non-prod loop. Prod reads stay
167	fast for metrics and metadata, but shrink during the transition: because the engineer's access is the
168	agent's access, from phase 1 the engineer too loses raw logs and configuration of services not yet
169	redacted or moved to runtime secrets. Configuration values come from the IaC code instead (layer 1
170	above); raw logs that may hold customer data need an L3-data grant. The data owner is not on the
171	on-call schedule, so at night the grant is approved by the on-call approver alone and the data owner
172	reviews it the next working day [design]; the wait still counts against S7. This is
173	the largest cost of the first months. Compliance gets least privilege that is enforced.
174	
175	---
176	
177	## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls
178	
179	**Principle.** Agent-side controls are hygiene, not the boundary. They are central, versioned in git
180	and the same for everyone. Defaults are safe; overrides are measured. The session that reads
181	untrusted content holds as little power as possible (📖 R6.1.2).
182	
183	**On Papaya's stack**
184	
185	- **Delivery:** server-managed settings (available on Team, 📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. With MDM, also
186	  an endpoint file; by default one managed source supplies most keys, so the two must carry the same
187	  keys or use `managedSourcesBehavior: "merge"` (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.4). MDM is unknown; both are prepared.
188	- **Baseline** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4). All keys 📖 at the row cited. Only the phase-1 subset in layer 8 ships first; the other keys (sandbox, `allowManagedHooksOnly`, credential denies, `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowedProviders`, `forceLoginOrgUUID`, the `ask` rule for WebFetch, and the other deny rules) arrive in phase 2 (OD4):
189	
190	  | Key | Value and reason |
191	  |---|---|
192	  | `permissions.defaultMode` | `default` (Manual). A default, not a lock: users can switch to auto; VS Code remembers the last pick (D1, R6.9.3). |
193	  | `permissions.allow` | Read-only commands Papaya uses, to cut prompts (R6.9.3). It contains no command listed in `sandbox.excludedCommands` (`aws`, `pulumi`, `serverless`): an allowed excluded command would run outside the sandbox, with `~/.aws` and the network, without a prompt (⚠️ inference from R1.2.6, R1.6.4) [design]. Cost: a prompt for every `aws` read. |
194	  | `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` | `true`, one rule set (D1, research 6.9.4 Q4; R1.2.5). Cost: project and user rules are ignored, so the managed set must carry every deny/ask rule projects need; prompts likely rise (⚠️ research 6.9.4 Q4). |
195	  | `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` | `"disable"`: removes bypass mode (P3a; R1.2.2). Auto mode, where a classifier approves instead of a person, stays available (D1) and is measured through `permission_mode`. |
196	  | `permissions.deny` / `ask` | Deny credential paths (R5.5.4; `Read(...)` syntax ⚠️ R1.8 #5). Ask for `WebFetch`, which the sandbox domain list does not limit (R1.6.2); cost: a prompt per fetch. The HIPAA template denies WebFetch (R5.5.4); "ask" is a deliberate deviation so that documentation lookups still work. |
197	  | `requiredMinimumVersion` | ≥ 2.1.285 for `allowedProviders` (R1.1.15), which also covers `--restricted` (2.1.248, R6.9.1b) and the plugin-pin fix (2.1.179, R6.2.7); ≥ 2.1.295 if any managed hook uses `onFailure: "block"` (R1.5.2); and ≥ the latest fixed advisory at rollout (R6.3.9). It does not end running sessions and fails open on a bad value (R1.1.13). |
198	  | `allowedProviders` + `forceLoginOrgUUID` | `["anthropic"]` + Papaya's org; closes most bypasses on **endpoint-managed** machines (R1.1.15). `forceLoginOrgUUID` checks claude.ai sign-ins only, not Claude Console sign-ins (R5.5.5); with it set, sessions on `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` or `apiKeyHelper` are refused (R1.11.3.11). |
199	  | `allowManagedHooksOnly` | `true` (R1.5.4). |
200	  | sandbox | `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, narrow `network.allowedDomains` locked by `network.allowManagedDomainsOnly`; `credentials` / `filesystem.denyRead` on `~/.aws`, which the sandbox can otherwise read (R1.6.3, R1.6.4). |
201	  | `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` | Agent's choice, to confirm (OQ-C) [design]: left at its default `true`. This widens D1's "Manual + read-only allowlist": every sandboxed command, writes in the working directory and calls to allowed domains included, runs without a prompt. Detail: sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, so in Manual mode prompts are for edits, unsandboxed commands and fetches, not every command (R5.5.5b). A deliberate choice: the sandbox (no `~/.aws`, allowlisted network) is the control for those commands. The HIPAA README says to set `false` if policy needs a person to approve each command (R5.5.5b); cost of `false`: a prompt per command. |
202	  | MCP, plugins | Layer 4. |
203	  | OTel | Exporter on, content flags `0` (R1.1.20, R5.5.4). |
204	
205	- **Trade-off on AWS credentials [design].** With `~/.aws` hidden from the sandbox, the plan is to
206	  list `aws`, `pulumi` and `serverless` in `sandbox.excludedCommands`. Excluded commands run "with
207	  full access" (📖 R1.6.4), which likely includes the network (⚠️ inference). How the list matches
208	  commands (prefix or text, and chained commands) is not researched (⚠️). This is worse than an
209	  egress channel: `pulumi preview` runs the Pulumi program and `serverless` loads its config and
210	  plugins, all code in the repo that the agent can edit, so excluding them lets repo code run
211	  outside the sandbox with network access and with `~/.aws` readable (⚠️ inference). For these
212	  commands the sandbox gives no protection. And an injected `aws` command could send out the SSO
213	  token cache itself. That token likely opens every role assigned to the engineer for the rest of the
214	  portal session (📖 R2.1.5; token reuse ⚠️ R2.2.2), probably including JIT or data-read grants added
215	  later in that session (⚠️ inference). Mitigations [design]: a short portal session (📖 R2.1.5); end
216	  the existing portal session and sign in fresh **before** a JIT or data-read grant is created
217	  (whether ending a session invalidates a token already stolen is unverified ⚠️; ending it does not
218	  end role sessions, 📖 R2.4.3); an SCP that denies writes to resources outside Papaya's organization using
219	  `aws:ResourceOrgID` (key 📖 R2.3.8), on every OU, since the token can be stolen from a non-prod
220	  session; legitimate writes to outside resources need exceptions (⚠️ not inventoried). That SCP only stops Papaya's own credentials writing to a
221	  foreign bucket; it does not stop a command that sends the token to a non-AWS endpoint or uses the
222	  attacker's credentials (⚠️ inference). Prefer running `pulumi` and `serverless` against real
223	  accounts only in CI; on laptops keep them to non-prod roles, and move them into the phase-3
224	  container. Residual risk: token theft during a session. It is accepted
225	  because the engineer holds no **standing** prod write and no **standing** PHI read; during a JIT
226	  or data-read window the protection is the process rule in layer 1 (D2). Stronger option, phase 3:
227	  a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
228	  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).
229	- **Session types:**
230	
231	  | Session | Identity | Flags | Enforcement |
232	  |---|---|---|---|
233	  | Daily development (laptop) | non-prod roles + `ProdReadMetadata` | baseline | Auto mode by choice (D1); `--restricted` recommended (D3). |
234	  | Incident analysis (laptop) | meant to be `ProdReadMetadata` only | `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"`, started in an empty scratch directory, not the repo [design] | Process rule (D3, research 6.9.4 Q1–Q2). No WebFetch, and file tools confined to the working directory (📖 R6.9.1b); Edit/Write are excluded only if `--tools` acts as an exclusive list (⚠️ unverified), but Bash can still write in its working directory (📖 R1.6.3) and call any role in the cache. |
235	  | CI agent (hosted runner) | own GitHub App token; never `production` | `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`; all rules in a managed-settings file on the runner | Workflow file under CODEOWNERS (D3, research 6.9.4 Q5). The file is advisory if `Bash` is in `--tools` (layer 5). |
236	  | JIT terminal | JIT grant | no agent | Process rule (D2). |
237	  | Auto-mode environment (phase 3) | non-prod only | auto encouraged | D1 option (c). |
238	
239	- **Phase-1 interim posture:** the sandbox and credential denies arrive in phase 2 (OD4), so for
240	  the first 30–60 days `~/.aws` is readable and the network is open to every Bash command; in auto
241	  mode the classifier is the only gate. Impact is bounded because standing prod write is removed in
242	  phase 1 (layer 1), but token theft is easier in this window.
243	- **Hard limits:** Bash rules are not a boundary (📖 R1.2.6); hooks fail open unless
244	  `"onFailure": "block"` (📖 R1.5.2); `--restricted` cannot be forced by a setting (📖 R6.9.1), and a `PATH` wrapper on laptops can be bypassed (⚠️ R6.9.1c);
245	  on laptops **without MDM**, a different login, an API key or a `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_*` variable skips
246	  server-managed settings, `allowedProviders` included (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ R1.8 #3, G11). So S5's
247	  "nobody can turn off all prompts unnoticed" is likely unreachable without MDM (⚠️).

268	## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level
269	
270	**Principle.** The level is set by the damage a change can do. One default path above non-prod: a
271	reviewed PR applied by the pipeline, with the JIT fallback (layer 7) as the only other write path.
272	The approver reviews the code change that will be applied. Every prod change needs two people, and
273	no more by default: one who makes it and one who approves it (until OQ-A is answered, the
274	cross-team process rule below can need more); the on-call backup only replaces an
275	unavailable primary (OD2). Higher risk narrows **who** may approve (the owners of that path), not how
276	many. Separately, any prod diff that looks risky stops the deploy, whatever its level; that adds a
277	second approval by an owner of the same stack, which keeps it to two people (OD8). Agent's reading
278	of OD8 [design], to confirm: the original author opens the approval PR and the first approver
279	approves it; if the first approver is unavailable, another owner of the stack approves, which makes
280	three people (open question OQ-B). Two edge cases: GitHub accepts one on-call group member for
281	files of several owner teams (OD9, 📖 R3.2.7), so "an approval from each domain team" on a
282	cross-team PR is a process rule only, and an interim default of the agent [design] until OQ-A; whether such PRs should be split is an open question for the
283	owner (OQ-A, below). A real-data read is not a change and has its own rule, L3-data. Incidents use the same
284	path with faster people, not fewer security checks.
285	
286	| Level | What | Examples | Approval | Path |
287	|---|---|---|---|---|
288	| **L0** | Read: non-prod anything; prod metadata | metrics, redacted logs | none | read-only identity |
289	| **L1** | Change in non-prod | deploy a branch to dev; `pulumi preview` on non-prod (needs state-write permission on a DIY S3 backend, 📖 R4.3.3) | author only | non-prod roles or PR pipeline |
290	| **L2** | Routine prod change in code | Lambda timeout/memory, ECS desired count, release | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher | PR → `main` → deploy workflow |
291	| **L3** | High-risk prod change | IAM/SCP; replace/delete of stateful resources; network; `.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/**`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`, `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, plugin/MCP catalogue and the rest of the canonical list in layer 5; advisory policy finding | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher. L3 paths (workflow and agent-config files, catalogue, stacks that hold only IAM/SCP): the L3 owner team. L3 content inside a domain file (an IAM statement in `serverless.yml`, a stateful delete): the stack's owner, then the risk stop (OD8). In incidents: the on-call approver for deployable paths (OD9); paths that define the process (CODEOWNERS, agent config, catalogue, workflows) wait for the L3 owner team | same path; for IaC changes the risk stop also applies; workflow and agent-config files have no prod diff |
292	| **L3-JIT** | Break-glass | ECS force-redeploy while Actions is down | on-call approver ≠ requester (Options §4b); outside incidents, an owner of the service ≠ requester [design]; agent's reading of OD9: the on-call approver counts as owner of the service in the request [design] | layer 7 |
293	| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | an approver ≠ requester and an agreement (GĐ-9); data-owner co-approval [design], beyond GĐ-9; at night, see layer 6 | layer 6 |
294	
295	`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for
296	the whole team (OD3). With code-owner review on, every PR, L2 included, needs an approval from an
297	owner of the files it touches (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7; per-file behaviour ⚠️ not a separate research row).
298	What differs at L3 is **which team** owns the path: L3 paths are owned in CODEOWNERS by a designated
299	L3 owner team (deployable L3 paths also by the on-call group, OD9), L2 paths by their domain team; and IaC changes at L3 meet the
300	risk stop. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files, so they are approved by
301	the stack's owners, not the L3 team (OD8); automated checks make up for this: IAM Access Analyzer
302	`check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and the Pulumi policy pack (📖 R4.2.2), both from phase 2 (layer 5). Cost: changes to `CLAUDE.md` (where D3 puts shared knowledge) need the L3 owner team, not
303	the domain team that edits it most.
304	
305	**On Papaya's stack**
306	
307	- **Gate = merge to `main`.** On Team, environment reviewers do not exist for private repos
308	  (📖 R3.1.2). Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
309	  approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
310	  push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). Branch up to date before merge, since there is
311	  no merge queue (⚠️ R4.6 #1; whether updating drops approvals is open, Options §8).
312	- **L3 approvals [design]:** CODEOWNERS plus code-owner review only, no path-based required
313	  reviewers rule. That rule (📖 R3.2.4) asks for approvals from specific teams, which the on-call
314	  group would not satisfy at night, and how it combines several teams is not researched (⚠️), so it
315	  would break OD9 or add a third person. GitHub stops the author from approving (📖 R3.3.1). A required check with a pinned source app (📖 R3.2.5), computed by a dedicated GitHub App, or by a workflow from the base branch that never checks out PR code and gets no secrets (likely `pull_request_target`, a privileged trigger, ⚠️) [design], adds what
316	  the rules cannot: for app-opened PRs it excludes the person who triggered the agent, and it counts
317	  only human approvals, since an app's approval might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3).
318	- **Who approves at night (OD9):** a fixed GitHub team, the on-call approvers, is listed as
319	  co-owner on every deployable path in CODEOWNERS (infrastructure and service code), next to the
320	  domain team. Agent's reading of OD9, to confirm: the group does **not** co-own the paths that
321	  define the process (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md` and agent config, catalogue); those stay
322	  with the L3 owner team only. If a broken workflow blocks a night fix, the pipeline counts as
323	  unavailable and the JIT fallback applies (layer 7). One primary and one backup from that team are on call. Technically any member can approve any
324	  path; by rule the primary approves and the backup only if the primary is unavailable (OD2).
325	  Membership is fixed, not changed per shift [design]. GitHub team membership is set in organization
326	  settings, not by a PR; managing it as code (e.g. with Pulumi's GitHub provider) and the audit
327	  event for a membership change are not researched (⚠️ G16). Meanwhile the layer-7 settings
328	  comparison includes the group's member list. Cost: an approval from any
329	  listed owner satisfies code-owner review (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days a member could approve
330	  another domain's PR, on or off shift. Mitigation [design]: process rule "approve another
331	  domain's PR only if it carries the `incident` label and you are on shift", and a monthly report of
332	  every cross-domain approval by group members on PRs without that label (layer 7). Whether Papaya's team size allows full coverage is unknown
333	  (§1, S7).
334	- **Risk stop [design]:** applies to every deploy, whatever the level. The deploy job previews prod;
335	  on stateful replace/delete, an IAM change, a network or security-group change, or an advisory
336	  policy finding it stops and posts the filtered preview. The original author opens a second PR that adds
337	  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml` (`<sha>` = the stopped commit) holding that SHA and the
338	  preview hash; the workflow does not open it, because the setting that lets Actions create and approve PRs stays
339	  off (📖 R3.3.3; ⚠️ R3.6 #3). CODEOWNERS on `deploy-approvals/<stack>/` names the owners of that stack and the
340	  on-call group (OD8, OD9). The approver is ≠ author and may be the first PR's approver, who now sees
341	  the prod diff. Merging it triggers the deploy on the new HEAD, which previews again and continues
342	  only if the hash matches the approved one; if another PR merged in between, the hash differs and
343	  the deploy stops again (Options §1; hash stability ⚠️ Options §8). Cost: while a stack is
344	  stopped, later merges to that stack stop too until a matching approval lands; in an incident, a
345	  risky change already waiting on `main` blocks the fix for the same stack until it is approved or
346	  reverted. A
347	  `mandatory` policy violation always blocks `pulumi up` (📖 R4.2.2): the fix is a code change, or a
348	  change to the policy pack through its own L3 PR. Preview output is filtered for
349	  outputs and secrets before it is posted (Options §1; ⚠️ R4.6 #2).
350	- **Merge approval = deploy approval** only if (⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c): `production`
351	  allows only `main`; only the reusable deploy workflow (under CODEOWNERS) references it; no ref/SHA
352	  inputs; no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers; one concurrency group
353	  per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4).
354	- **Pulumi:** PRs preview non-prod only, because a prod preview runs PR code with state-write and
355	  secret access (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). On `main`: prod preview, then `pulumi up` with the
356	  policy pack, which stops on a mandatory violation (📖 R4.2.2). Prod runs allow no `--skip-preview`
357	  (📖 R4.1.2) and no targeting, replace, `state`, `import`, `destroy` (⚠️ R4.6 #3, G12). Pulumi Cloud,
358	  if used: OIDC via `pulumi/auth-actions`, no stored token (📖 R4.1.4).
359	- **Serverless v4:** `serverless package`; `serverless diff --json` (sf-core ≥ 4.37.0), parsed by CI
360	  because differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2); `serverless deploy --package`
361	  (📖 R4.4.3); a least-privilege `deploymentRole`, which cannot be removed later and is usable by
362	  anyone who may operate the stack (📖 R4.4.5), so JIT roles get no stack-operation rights.
363	- **State:** writable by deploy roles (and possibly the drift role, layer 7); Pulumi
364	  secrets via `awskms` on a DIY backend (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #7).
365	- **k0s [design]:** manifests in the monorepo, applied by CI; no write RBAC for humans or agents in
366	  prod; read roles exclude logs and exec in namespaces with claim data (mechanism: G1). The risk
367	  stop is described for Pulumi and Serverless only; for k0s manifests (RBAC changes are the IAM
368	  equivalent) a `kubectl diff`-based stop is a candidate, not researched (⚠️ G1). Firebase deploys
369	  have no preview step in this design (⚠️ G2).
370	- **Incident lane:** label `incident`, on-call approver paged, security checks always run (S10), only
371	  slow unrelated tests skipped [design].
372	
373	**Example: Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m.** (Options §6)
374	
375	The incident responder is engineer E; the on-call approver is R (a backup replaces R only if R is
376	unavailable).
377	
378	1. E's incident-analysis session reads metrics and redacted logs and proposes `timeout` 30 → 90 s,
379	   memory 1024 → 2048 MB, and a larger visibility timeout on the source queue (ratio ⚠️ Options §8).
380	2. A second session (edit tools; not meant to use prod roles) edits `serverless.yml`, runs
381	   `serverless diff` on non-prod, and opens a PR labelled `incident` as E.
382	3. R, a co-owner of `serverless.yml` through the on-call group (OD9), reviews the diff. If R
383	   catches a missing queue change, R does not fix it (OD7): E pushes the fix, the stale approval is
384	   dismissed, and R approves again, one more review round (Options §6). E merges.
385	4. The deploy workflow packages, previews prod, finds no risky change, deploys with the OIDC role.
386	5. Estimate 11–46 min (⚠️ Options §6) against ≤ 30 min: measured first in rollout.
387	
388	**Audit evidence.** The PR (diff, approvers, checks); run log and preview artifact, exported because
389	retention is unverified (⚠️ G7); deploy-role CloudTrail events; all linked by commit SHA and run ID.
390	
391	**Cost / value.** One approver for every prod change, from the owners of the path; two approvals,
392	usually by the same approver, when the risk stop fires (agent's reading AR 1; OQ-B). Cross-team PRs: open (OQ-A). None in non-prod.
393	Compliance gets four-eyes enforced by GitHub. Gap: on Team the prod diff is not seen before apply.

434	## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening
435	
436	**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
437	least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
438	checks as human code (S10).
439	
440	**On Papaya's stack**
441	
442	- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
443	  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). Org default for `GITHUB_TOKEN` set to "restricted", `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
444	  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
445	  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
446	  deploys may need a stored credential in GitHub: a kubeconfig or token for k0s, a Firebase token or
447	  service-account key for Firebase Hosting. The owner accepts this as an exception to S2 = 0 until it
448	  is checked whether k0s and Firebase deploys can use OIDC (OD1, OD6). Conditions [design]:
449	  - stored only as an **environment secret of `production`**, never as a repository secret. Anyone
450	    with write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b), which would turn the exception into
451	    standing prod write for every engineer and their agent. Environment secrets and a deployment
452	    branch rule limited to `main` are available on Team for private repos (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3), and
453	    only the reviewed deploy workflow references the environment (layer 3);
454	  - the deploy job runs on GitHub-hosted runners. On self-hosted runners, jobs "are not run in an
455	    isolated container, even if they use environments", so environment secrets there must be

457	    compromised by untrusted code" from anyone who can open a PR, and runner groups limit only which

464	  - optionally a separate environment (e.g. `production-k0s`), limited to `main` and referenced
465	    only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy jobs cannot read these secrets

513	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
514	
515	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
516	Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
517	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
518	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
519	tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
520	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).
521	
522	**On Papaya's stack**
523	
524	- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
525	  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role from
526	    phase 1 (existing broad read roles are removed) and the SCP from phase 2
527	    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
528	    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
529	  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
530	  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
531	    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
532	  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
533	- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
534	  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. At night the data owner is not on call: the
535	  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day. This
536	  applies to non-PHI and PHI alike; for PHI the reader is still a human without an agent. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
537	  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
538	  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent (process rule, layer 1); the agent gets a
539	    redacted summary. This
540	    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
541	    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
542	  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9). Claim
543	    tables mix health, ID and bank data (research 1.11.4 L2), so a store that holds PHI is treated as
544	    PHI unless the agent reads a view or extract without PHI [design].
545	- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
546	  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
547	  1.11.4 L6).
548	- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default (sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, layer 2); the auto-mode
549	  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions and 5.7 % of 1,000 synthetic exfiltration
550	  attempts (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path
551	  (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no WebFetch, likely no edit tools (layer 2), and runs outside
552	  the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
553	  commands (layer 2), including the SSO token cache; "no standing write, no PHI read" limits what
554	  the token opens, except during a JIT or data-read window (layer 2 mitigations). Shared knowledge
555	  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is exempt from the protected-path rules unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
556	- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
557	  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed
558	  (GĐ-3, unconfirmed).
559	- **Non-prod:** no prod copies (S11). A scan of non-prod stores runs at the start of phase 1 (tool:
560	  G4); a store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule (GĐ-14: until cleaned, non-prod follows the GĐ-9 data-read rule). Cost: until scanned, that store is
561	  not part of the free loop.
562	- **Local stores:** transcripts and memory hold what the agent read (research 1.11.4); set
563	  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).
564	- **Cross-border (Vietnam example):** processing data collected in Vietnam on a platform abroad is a
565	  transfer (📖 R5.4.5); agent flows, including employee names in logs and transcripts, update the
566	  transfer impact assessment (⚠️ R5.7 #4, needs Papaya legal).
567	
568	**Audit evidence.** SCP/IAM text as the written access rule for sensitive data (📖 R5.4.3; ⚠️ R5.7 #5);
569	data-read requests and the data-read role's CloudTrail; planted-injection reports (layer 8); non-prod
570	scan results (S11).
571	
572	**Cost / value.** Debugging with redacted and synthetic data; a request for the rare real-data read.
573	Compliance gets "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM for AWS stores (fully from phase 2;
574	actions ⚠️ G13) and by process
575	elsewhere, and a record per exception (S9).
576	
577	---
578	
579	## Layer 7 — Observability, audit, incident response and break-glass
580	
581	**Principle.** One tamper-evident evidence chain per prod change. One routed alert channel with a
582	named on-call, approvers included. Unapproved change is detected (drift, reconciliation). Break-glass
583	is approved before use, time-boxed and reconciled after.
584	
585	**On Papaya's stack**
586	
587	- **Audit stores:**
588	  - organization CloudTrail to a log-archive account with integrity validation (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4,
589	    R2.6.5); change records ≥ 6 years; raw-log retention for Papaya's compliance owner (⚠️ R5.7 #2).

604	  approved before apply (S3). Actor: `onBehalfOf.userId` where present, else session name plus

607	  prod secrets in state, which is noted (⚠️ R4.6 #2). Scheduled `pulumi preview --refresh
608	  --expect-no-changes` or `pulumi refresh --preview-only` (📖 R4.1.1, R4.3.1, R4.3.2). On a DIY S3
609	  backend, preview needs state-write permission (📖 R4.3.3); whether a refresh preview writes more
610	  than locks is open (⚠️ R4.6 #2, G14). So either the drift role gets state write (and the same
611	  trust care as the deploy role), or Pulumi Cloud drift detection is used (📖 R4.3.2, Pro+). The
612	  latter runs on Pulumi Deployments, which holds credentials to prod, so it re-opens a side path that
613	  layer 5 excludes and needs the same trust narrowing and audit (📖 R4.4.9; ⚠️ R4.6 #6). CloudFormation
614	  drift detection, explicitly set properties only (📖 R4.4.6). No auto-remediation: it is an unreviewed
615	  `pulumi up --refresh` (📖 R4.3.2). Each finding gets an actor and a ticket.
616	- **On-call:** phase 1 delivers the named approver schedule (primary + backup engineers, 24/7), as
617	  decided in framing round 1, and, because of OD7, a minimal incident-responder schedule; the
618	  latter extends that decision. The primary approves; the backup steps in only if the primary is
619	  unavailable (OD2). On-call approvers only approve during their shift; the fix is written by an
620	  incident responder (OD7). Alert routing and the
621	  rest of on-call follow in phase 2 (tools: G5); in phase 1 the responder calls the approver by phone from the published schedule.
622	- **Break-glass = JIT fallback** [design unless marked]:
623	
624	  | Step | Rule |
625	  |---|---|
626	  | When | The PR path cannot be used: operation not in IaC and no runbook; GitHub/Actions down; pipeline broken. The approver refuses JIT for anything expressible in IaC while the pipeline works, and records why. |
627	  | Request | Command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub. |
628	  | Approval | On-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant (Options §4b; OD7; backup rule OD2). |
629	  | Grant | `InfraOperator-<service>`; role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). Deleting the assignment likely stops only new sessions (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3), so the real window can approach 2 h; ending the portal session does not end role sessions (📖 R2.4.3). An immediate stop needs the revocation SCP, which must keep the user blocked for at least 12 h (📖 R2.4.4). |
630	  | Execution | The grant goes to the requester (the incident responder), who types the commands; no agent in that terminal (D2). D2 said the on-call person runs them; OD7 moves that to the responder, since on-call engineers only approve. |
631	  | After | A job compares CloudTrail writes in the window with the list; a codify PR within a fixed deadline (as soon as GitHub is back); drift detection until it merges. |
632	  | Identity Center outage | Emergency SAML federation to roles, built and tested in advance (📖 R2.1.11; ⚠️ R2.9 #2); no user mapped until an approved activation, which is alerted. |

658	## Layer 8 — Governance and rollout
659	
660	**Principle.** Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date. Policies are files changed by

662	attacks.

### 2.9 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **On a laptop, an agent that calls the AWS CLI/SDK directly is indistinguishable from the
   engineer.**
   - **Why:** it uses the same SSO cache, and that cache reaches every role assigned to the
     engineer (2.2.1, 2.2.2). App ID is a client hint (2.2.3). Source identity is trustworthy only
     when the IdP asserts it (2.5.4).
   - **Consequence:** a separate "agent" permission set alone does not separate the two. The
     agent can still use the engineer's other roles from the same cache.
   - **The one native, server-set signal is the AWS MCP Server** (2.2.4, 2.2.5). Calls through it
     carry `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` / `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP`, usable in SCPs. They are absent (or
     false) on direct calls (2.2.5). So the signal is a control only if the agent **cannot make
     direct calls at all**.
   - **Untested design idea, not in the docs (⚠️):** an agent-only role that denies requests not
     made through MCP. AWS documents only the reverse ("deny when via MCP"). The idea helps only if
     the agent cannot reach the engineer's other credentials:
     - **With SigV4,** the local proxy reads the AWS CLI credentials as the same OS user, so this
       needs the proxy outside the agent's sandbox (1.6).
     - **With OAuth,** the MCP path itself needs no AWS CLI credentials. But the MCP client still
       holds the OAuth token, and the agent must still be kept away from the engineer's own SSO
       cache (⚠️). There is also no multi-profile.

     Without that condition, a separate role adds no control. Also to test: whether
     `aws___run_script` and `aws___get_presigned_url` downloads carry the keys. A presigned-URL
     download is made directly by the client.
   - **The decisive layer remains no standing prod-write assignment for humans** (#2). Then
     nothing running on the laptop can write to prod outside an approved, time-boxed window.
     **Inside that window,** any process on the laptop can use the grant. This is a residual risk
     to state openly.
     *(2026-11-08: the owner chose a process control for this window, see 6.6 D2.)*
2. **Changing prod: the default path is a pipeline; human write access is the exception, via JIT.**
   - **Default path:** humans hold no prod-write rights. Changes go through CI with a deploy role.
     The named-human approval happens at the CI gate (GitHub Environments, Topic 3).
   - **JIT, for the rest:** when a human needs write access (manual operations, incidents), it
     comes from a JIT assignment. AWS has no native request/approve feature (2.4.1). The options:
     - a partner product (2.4.1);
     - the TEAM sample (2.4.1b);
     - a small home-built flow on `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (2.4.2).
   - **Audit evidence:** CloudTrail records the **grant**, and its caller is the automation role.
     It does **not** record the approver. The approver's identity lives in the approval system
     (GitHub, Linear, the partner tool, TEAM). It must be linked to the grant, for example by
     request ID, and kept as audit evidence (⚠️ design).
   - **Incidents:** under GĐ-8 the incident path is the same flow with a fast approver, not a
     bypass.
   - **Outage path:** the emergency direct-federation path (2.1.11) is for an Identity Center
     outage, and needs its own approval and alerting.
3. **Revocation is slow by design.**
   - Role sessions outlive portal sessions and assignments (2.4.3). IAM's revoke button does not
     apply to permission-set roles (2.4.6).
   - Prod permission sets should use the **1-hour minimum** session duration (2.1.4).
   - Pre-deploy the `identitystore:userId` Deny SCP on the prod OU (2.4.4), and keep the
     `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as an org-wide kill switch (2.4.6). This is an inference (⚠️):
     scope it by `aws:PrincipalArn` so that workload roles are not hit.
   - Set the portal session length deliberately (2.1.5, 2.1.6), including the IdP session,
     which can silently extend it.
4. **SCPs are the guardrail the agent cannot edit, but only in member accounts.** Examples:
   - protect the org trail and the log archive (2.6.2);
   - deny region drift;
   - deny data-plane reads on PHI buckets and queues, except for the application roles **and**
     the approved JIT read path that GĐ-9 allows (`aws:PrincipalArn`; tenant scoping via ABAC
     session tags, 2.1.8). This supports 1.11.4 L3–L4;
   - deny destructive actions when `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` is true (2.2.5). On its own this is
     bypassed by direct CLI calls (#1), so it is a second layer, not a control.

   Constraints:
   - Keep everything out of the management account (2.3.2, 2.3.7).
   - Deny-list SCPs sit on `FullAWSAccess` (2.3.4b).
   - Limits are 10 direct attachments per target and 10,240 characters each (2.3.4).
   - RCPs add an outside-the-org boundary for S3, SQS, KMS, Secrets Manager and Logs, but not for
     Aurora, Lambda or SNS (2.3.6).
5. **Audit trail for Compliance:**
   - **Trail:** an organization trail to a separate log-archive account, with integrity validation
     and a locked-down bucket (2.6.2, 2.6.4, 2.6.5).
   - **Retention:** decide it explicitly. The default is indefinite, and MFA delete excludes
     lifecycle rules (2.6.5).
   - **Data events:** only where they matter, because of cost (2.6.3): PHI buckets, prod Lambda
     invoke, prod SQS.
   - **No CloudTrail Lake** (2.6.6).
   - **Who did it:** use `onBehalfOf.userId` in CloudTrail where present. Otherwise use the
     session name plus a lookup in the directory (⚠️, 2.5.3). The session name changes when the
     username changes, so it is not a stable key. (`identitystore:UserId` is a policy condition
     key, not a CloudTrail field.)
   - **MCP events:** do not assume AWS MCP Server events are in the trail until the selector
     question is answered (2.5.5).
   - **Aurora:** SQL is invisible to CloudTrail (2.7.1). Use Database Activity Streams or pgaudit,
     alert on the RDS events about lost records, and treat that stream as PHI (2.7.2, 2.7.3).
   - **Same gap for shell sessions:** ECS Exec and SSM shell sessions likely have the same issue
     (⚠️ not researched, 2.10).
6. **Policy changes in Pulumi PRs can be checked mechanically.** `check-no-new-access` in CI makes
   "this PR widens IAM" a visible, reviewable fact (2.8.1; ties to Topics 3–4).

### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
     is per deployment job and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, an empty bypass
       list (3.2.2–3.2.4);
     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3).
   - **Prerequisite on both plans: the branch rule alone does not mean "only merged, approved
     code reaches prod".** Every workflow on `main` passes a "main only" rule, whatever its trigger
     (3.4.5c). So all of the following must also hold:
     - only reviewed deploy workflows may reference `production`, enforced by CODEOWNERS on
       `.github/workflows` and a CI check;
     - deploy workflows take no ref or SHA input, and deploy the commit they run on;
     - no `production` job runs on `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`.
       A `schedule` deploy of the current `main` commit is acceptable only if it deploys that
       commit and takes no input;
     - preferably, the `sub` claim is pinned to the reusable deploy workflow (`job_workflow_ref`,
       3.4.5).

     Under these conditions, merge approval equals deploy approval on Team.
   - **Admins remain a gap.** Admins and holders of "edit repository rules" can edit rulesets,
     environments and the OIDC `sub` customisation. This is mostly logged, not prevented (3.1.4,
     3.2.2, 3.4.5). So: few admins, periodic access review, and alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`,
     `environment.update_protection_rule`, `environment.remove_protection_rule`,
     `environment.delete` and `protected_branch.policy_override`.
   - **UI changes to the branch policy may not be audited** (⚠️, 3.1.4). A deleted
     `production` environment is likely recreated without protection by the next workflow
     that references it. The deletion itself is logged (⚠️ inference, 3.1.4). So a scheduled
     job should also compare the live environment configuration with the expected one, as
     drift detection (⚠️: the REST endpoint was not researched).
   - **GĐ-5 holds only on Enterprise.** It should go back to the framing as a correction and an
     open question for Papaya.
2. **OIDC trust must pin the repository, the gate and, where possible, the workflow** (3.4.2–3.4.5c):
   - **AWS:** prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the repo's
     `sub` format (3.4.4). Ideally a customised `sub` includes `job_workflow_ref`, because AWS
     cannot test other claims (3.4.5).
   - **GCP:** the attribute condition must restrict to the GitHub organization (required by
     Google). It can also test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` and `event_name` directly (3.4.5b).
   - **Non-prod:** roles trust a separate environment.
   - **Secrets:** prod credentials never live in repository secrets, because anyone with write
     access can read those (3.5.3b). This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
   or a custom check whose source app is pinned. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
   requests" stays **off** (3.3.3).
4. **CI agents and policy files:** on standard GitHub-hosted runners, an agent with shell access
   has root, so Claude Code managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the
   Topic 1 question). The real limits for a CI agent are:
   - the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3);
   - **no** `environment: production` in any agent workflow, so it gets no prod OIDC trust
     (3.4.5c);
   - the base-branch config restore in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9).

   Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring persistence risks (3.5.2).
5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA evidence
   needs longer, so it must be exported periodically (JSON or CSV, within the export limits, ✅)
   or streamed (⚠️ not researched; may be Enterprise-only).

PR code can therefore apply to non-prod, which is acceptable because non-prod holds no real data (GĐ-14); - **prod deploy:** trusts `environment:production` only; - **prod drift check:** a separate read role trusted only from a dedicated `drift` environment restricted to `main`. It must not be able to change state, so state writes stay with the deploy role (⚠️ whether refresh preview needs lock writes, see 4.7). It probably needs `kms:Decrypt`, or Pulumi Cloud stack read, to read state that contains secrets. The drift job can then read prod secrets, which must be noted and restricted. 3. **Close the bypass paths inside the tools:** - **`serverless deploy function`** changes code **and configuration** outside CloudFormation. The change persists after the next deploy (4.4.4). In prod, deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` **and** `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` to every principal except the CloudFormation `deploymentRole`. - This works only if `deploymentRole` is set. Otherwise CloudFormation uses the caller's credentials, and the CI role would need those rights itself (4.4.5). - Using `aws:CalledVia` for this is an option (⚠️ untested). - **Least-privilege `deploymentRole`:** it cannot be removed later, and anyone who may operate the stack can use it (4.4.5). Add a `stackPolicy` for stateful resources. - **Pulumi:** prod workflows use an **allowlist** of commands and flags (`preview`, `up` without `--target`, `--target-replace`, `--replace`, `--exclude` or `--skip-preview`). IAM cannot tell `pulumi` commands apart: the deploy role can write state anyway. So keeping state-changing commands (`state …`, `import`, `destroy`, `stack rm`) out of prod runs is enforced only by the workflow allowlist plus CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8). Any other use needs a separately approved run. 4. **Policy as code where the agent can't switch it off.** - **Enforcement point:** the policy that counts is the one evaluated during `up` on `main` (4.2.4). - Prefer Pulumi Cloud policy groups (Essentials+) if Papaya is on Pulumi Cloud, and limit who can run `pulumi policy disable`. - Otherwise use `--policy-pack` in a CODEOWNERS-protected reusable workflow (4.2.3). - **No `remediate` level in prod** (4.2.4). - **Serverless:** the CloudFormation template from `sls package` can be checked by a CI policy tool (⚠️ tool not researched). Add IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` on changed policies (2.8.1). 5. **Drift is a compliance signal: it means an unreviewed change happened.** - **Pulumi:** scheduled `pulumi refresh --preview-only`, or `pulumi preview --refresh --expect-no-changes`. Without `--refresh`, a preview compares only against recorded state and cannot see drift (4.3.1). Or use Pulumi Cloud drift detection (Pro+), **with auto-remediation off in prod**, because it runs an unreviewed `up` (4.3.2). - **Serverless:** scheduled CloudFormation drift detection, with its coverage limits (4.4.6). It may not catch a `deploy function` code change (⚠️, 4.7). - Every drift finding maps to a CloudTrail actor (2.5) and an incident or ticket. 6. **Third-party credential paths must be closed or put under the same gate** (4.4.9). Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard Providers each hold a path to prod. - **Default:** do not use them for prod. - **If they are used:** their AWS trust and their admin roles must be as narrow as the GitHub `production` path, and audited (Pulumi Cloud audit logs need Pro+, 4.3.5). 7. **State and secrets:** - **State buckets:** Pulumi state and Serverless state buckets are prod-sensitive stores (encrypted secrets, resource outputs). Restrict them to the deploy roles (4.3.3, 4.4.1). - **Pulumi secrets:** use `awskms` as the secrets provider on a DIY backend (4.3.4). - **Serverless secrets:** resolve them at runtime, not baked into templates (⚠️ 4.4.7). - **Serverless License Key:** keep it in SSM per account, read by the deploy role (≥ 4.4.19). This avoids a long-lived GitHub secret (4.4.8, 3.5.3b).
